title: Convex Hull
description: Find the smallest convex boundary that encloses a set of points

blocks.text: The convex hull of a set of points is the smallest convex shape that contains all of them. It is one of the most famous problems in computational geometry and a building block for many others.
We will focus on Andrew monotone chain algorithm, which is clean, fast, and easy to get right.
Picture hammering a nail into each point, stretching a rubber band around all of them, and letting go. The band snaps tight around the outermost points. That taut outline is the convex hull.

blocks.caption: The convex hull is the shape a rubber band forms around the outer points

blocks.text: Convex means the boundary never dents inward: every interior point sits inside, and the outline only ever turns one way as you walk around it.

The key insight is that the hull boundary only makes turns in a single direction. So if we walk the points in order and ever make a turn the wrong way, the previous point cannot be on the hull and we remove it.
This is exactly the orientation test again. Deciding which points to keep is just repeatedly asking whether the last three points turn the correct way.
The monotone chain algorithm sorts the points, then builds the hull in two halves.

blocks.caption: Sort the points, build the lower and upper hulls, popping any wrong turn

items: Sort all points by x, breaking ties by y
Sweep left to right to build the lower hull
Sweep right to left to build the upper hull
While adding a point, pop the last one if it makes a non left turn
Join the two chains to get the full hull

blocks.text: The cross helper returns the turn direction of three points, and we pop whenever the turn is not strictly correct.
The cost is dominated by the sort, which is O(n log n). The two sweeps that build the hull are linear, since each point is pushed and popped at most once.

Decide about boundary points:

The comparison in the pop test decides whether points lying exactly on an edge are kept. Use a strict or non strict comparison depending on whether your problem wants collinear boundary points included.
The hull is a springboard for many geometric queries.

items: Finding the two farthest points, which always lie on the hull
Measuring the smallest enclosing box or width of a point set
Collision and reachability questions in games and robotics

blocks.text: Because it reduces a cloud of points to just its meaningful outer boundary, the convex hull simplifies many harder problems.
